title: A Vision-Language Pre-training Model-Guided Approach for Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning

C-a.quote: CLIP-Fed combines pre-aggregation model clustering and post-aggregation backdoor purification to jointly enhance defense robustness, reducing dependence on homogeneous client data distributions.
C-a.locator: Sec. 1, contribution 1; both stages carry a defense purpose in that sentence and the pipeline order is in the stage names. The purposes are restated separately at Sec. 1, "clustering filters out malicious updates, and post-aggregation purification uses a global model adjustment to enhance robustness under Non-IID conditions", and the aggregation step between them is given explicitly at Sec. 3, "After model clustering, CLIP-Fed performs global model aggregation as specified in Eq. (2)". The purification stage itself has two constituents, "a global purification mechanism combining prototype contrastive learning and knowledge distillation" (Sec. 1), both defense-purposed. AMENDMENT 3 EXCLUDES NOTHING HERE: the server-dataset construction from a multimodal LLM plus frequency analysis is purposed for trigger coverage and for avoiding client data, "which enhances the dataset's coverage against diverse backdoor triggers without accessing client data" (Sec. 1), so it is support machinery rather than a counted mechanism, and the count reaches two without it

C-b.quote: clustering process enables CLIPFed to eliminate most malicious models prior to aggregation, it is Trovato et al. acknowledged that the identified benign clusters may still contain some residual malicious models.
C-b.locator: Sec. 3 (the extracted sentence carries a running-head artifact, "Trovato et al.", from the paper's ACM template); this is RESIDUAL COVERAGE stated as the reason for the second stage, the same kind as RKD's. The regime-level reason is separate and is stated as a deficiency of the first stage's whole family, "clustering model parameters [5, 20, 21], while it is highly dependent on the homogeneous data distribution of FL" (Sec. 2), and the paper closes the argument by explaining why the second stage does not inherit that dependence, "heterogeneous client data distributions primarily affected the filtering of malicious models before aggregation, while CLIP-Fed's backdoor purification strategy was decoupled from model aggregation" (Sec. 4)

C-c.quote: Table 1 presented a comparison of Main Task Accuracy (MA) and Attack Success Rate (ASR) across various methods under distinct data distributions and backdoor attacks.
C-c.locator: Sec. 4.1; the assembled framework's MA and ASR are reported over CIFAR-10, CIFAR-10-LT and CIFAR-100 against BadNets, DBA, LayerAttack and AFA, at 20/30/40% malicious clients and against FLTrust, FoolsGold, FEDCPA, FedAvg and FLAME, with the composed claim at Sec. 1, "CLIP-Fed achieves an average reduction in ASR, i.e., 2.03% on CIFAR-10 and 1.35% on CIFAR-10-LT, while improving the average MA by 7.92% and 0.48%, respectively"

C-d.quote: The results indicated that individually applying either feature extractor retraining or global model knowledge distillation could partially eliminate the association between trigger patterns and target labels, thereby mitigating backdoor effects.
C-d.locator: Sec. 4.2 Ablation Study, Table 2, arms CLIP-Fed w/o FR ("without feature extractor rectification") and CLIP-Fed w/o KD ("without knowledge distillation"), each with full MA/ASR on three datasets and four attacks. CODED YES UNDER RULE 4, on the w/o-FR arm: the paper's own account makes the rectification upstream of the distillation, "we rectify the global model's feature extractor to correct class prototype deviations that are caused by backdoor samples, while decoupling strong correlations between trigger patterns and target labels. To this end, we align the logits distributions of CLIP and the global model through knowledge transfer to further remove residual backdoor associations" (Sec. 1), so removing FR holds the distillation fixed and changes the model state that reaches it. THE COMPETING READING IS RECORDED: the two constituents are also described as a single combined objective, "prototype contrastive loss and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence" (Sec. 1), on which reading the arms drop one term of a joint loss and vary the terminal stage rather than an upstream input, and the PRE-AGGREGATION CLUSTERING -- the one unambiguously upstream stage -- is never varied in any arm

C-e.quote: heterogeneous client data distributions primarily affected the filtering of malicious models before aggregation, while CLIP-Fed’s backdoor purification strategy was decoupled from model aggregation.
C-e.locator: Sec. 4; the claim assigns the observed non-IID behaviour to one constituent and exempts the other, which is a mechanism-attribution claim about the composition. A second, measured one is the C-d quotation on the two purification constituents, and a third is at Sec. 3 on the clustering stage's residue

coder_note:
C-d = YES ON RULE 4 AND THE ROW WOULD BE A PRIMARY WITHOUT IT, SO THE REASONING IS RECORDED IN FULL. The unambiguous upstream stage in this paper is the pre-aggregation clustering, and NO arm varies it: both ablation arms live inside the post-aggregation purification. Read that way the paper only ever varies its downstream stage, which is the DROPlet direction, and CLIP-Fed becomes the frame's fifth primary. What saves the C-d is internal to the purification module: the paper describes feature-extractor rectification as acting on the feature extractor and distillation as aligning logits to remove what rectification leaves behind, and features feed logits, so w/o-FR plausibly holds a downstream mechanism fixed while removing what reaches it. Rule 4 mandates the benefit of the doubt for exactly that configuration and rule 3 points the same way, so YES is the coded value; a reader who treats the two as terms of one joint loss gets a fourth-to-fifth primary instead. This is the second row after FLTG where the primary count turns on a single judgment call, and both are recorded so the rate can be recomputed under either policy.

RESIDUAL COVERAGE IS NOW THE MOST COMMON PAIRING REASON IN THE FRAME. RKD, DROP, DP2Guard and CLIP-Fed all justify a second stage by naming what the first one leaves behind -- models that survive inside a benign cluster, adversaries that alternate across rounds, correlations that survive feature rectification. That is worth reporting in A5's taxonomy as the modal kind rather than as one of five, because it bears on the paper's argument: a composition motivated by residue is exactly the case where the downstream stage's behaviour depends on what the upstream stage passed through, and therefore exactly the case where the identifying contrast is most needed and its absence most costly.

DOMAIN NOTE: this is the frame's first defense whose downstream stage is a FOUNDATION-MODEL-GUIDED repair rather than a filter, aggregation rule or reweighting -- the composed system's second half is prototype alignment against CLIP embeddings on a server dataset synthesized by a multimodal LLM. It is included correctly under the frozen screen, and it widens the frame's notion of what a defense stage can be. The template artifact in the extracted text ("Trovato et al." appearing mid-sentence, an unreplaced ACM sample-template running head) is noted in the C-b locator so a reader is not misled into thinking the quotation was garbled by the extractor.
